hints: Rewrite every double-angle term using $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$.
Factor the numerator and denominator, cancel their common factor where defined, and simplify the remaining ratio.
walkthrough:
Recall the double angle trigonometric identities:
$$\cos 2\theta = 1 - 2\sin^2\theta \implies 1 - \cos 2\theta = 2\sin^2\theta$$
$$\cos 2\theta = 2\cos^2\theta - 1 \implies 1 + \cos 2\theta = 2\cos^2\theta$$
$$\sin 2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta$$

Substitute these identities into the numerator of $\mathrm{f}(\theta)$:
$$\text{Numerator} = (1 - \cos 2\theta) + \sin 2\theta = 2\sin^2\theta + 2\sin\theta\cos\theta = 2\sin\theta(\sin\theta + \cos\theta)$$

Substitute these identities into the denominator of $\mathrm{f}(\theta)$:
$$\text{Denominator} = (1 + \cos 2\theta) + \sin 2\theta = 2\cos^2\theta + 2\sin\theta\cos\theta = 2\cos\theta(\cos\theta + \sin\theta)$$

Cancel the common non-zero factor $2(\sin\theta + \cos\theta)$:
$$\mathrm{f}(\theta) = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \tan\theta$$
This establishes the identity $\mathrm{f}(\theta) = \tan\theta$.

ai_rubric.Trigonometric Identities: Applies double-angle formulae and expresses the entire fraction in terms of $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$. Derives the displayed intermediate equation. The final result is $f(\theta)=\tan\theta$.

hints: Substitute $\theta=\pi/4$ and $\theta=\pi/6$ with exact cosine values, then combine the logarithms into the required single logarithm.
walkthrough:
Replace $\mathrm{f}(\theta)$ with $\tan\theta$ in the definite integral:
$$\int_{\frac{1}{6}\pi}^{\frac{1}{4}\pi} \mathrm{f}(\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta = \int_{\frac{1}{6}\pi}^{\frac{1}{4}\pi} \tan\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta$$

Subtract the lower limit value from the upper limit value:
$$\text{Integral} = \left(-\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\right) - \left(-\ln\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\right) = \ln(\sqrt{2}) - \ln\left(\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\right)$$

Combine using the logarithm quotient rule $\ln A - \ln B = \ln(A/B)$:
$$\ln\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2/\sqrt{3}}\right) = \ln\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2} \times \sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = \ln\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{6}}{2}\right) = \ln\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{6}{4}}\right) = \ln\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}}\right)$$

Rewrite the square root as a fractional power and bring the exponent out front:
$$\ln\left(\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^{1/2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\ln\dfrac{3}{2}$$
This confirms the exact result.
